description: The basic major triad. Commonly used in pop, folk, and country music where simple and stable harmony is required. Often swapped for a richer voicing like maj7 or 6 in genres that favor smoother, more harmonically complex colour
The basic minor triad. Common across nearly every genre; frequently the vi chord in a major-key progression. Often swapped for min7 in genres that favor a smoother, less stark minor colour

A dominant seventh chord — a major triad with a flattened seventh added. Core to blues and rock, where it's used on any chord (not just the V) for a gritty, unresolved tension. Also foundational to jazz harmony, where it functions as the V7 in ii-V-I progressions and applied dominants, and common in reggae for a relaxed, slightly unresolved color over the skank rhythm; in traditional harmony it strongly pulls toward resolving a fourth up (e.g. G7 to C)

A major seventh chord — a major triad with the natural seventh added. Common in jazz, soul, and softer pop/R&B ballads for a lush, dreamy, unresolved colour; less gritty than a dominant seventh and rarely used in blues or hard rock

A minor seventh chord — a minor triad with a flattened seventh added. Very common in jazz, funk, soul, and R&B for a smoother, mellower colour than a plain minor triad; frequently used for the ii chord in a ii-V-I progression

A suspended second chord — the third replaced with a major second, removing the major/minor quality entirely for an open, ambiguous sound. Common in pop, rock, and acoustic/folk playing, often used as a passing or decorative chord that resolves back to a major or minor triad

A suspended fourth chord — the third replaced with a perfect fourth, creating tension that typically wants to resolve down to a major or minor triad. Common in rock, pop, and worship music, often played briefly before resolving to the underlying chord (e.g. Dsus4 to D)

A diminished triad — a minor triad with a flattened fifth, producing a tense, unstable sound. Used sparingly across genres, most often as a passing chord (e.g. the vii° in a major key) connecting two more stable chords, rarely held as a point of rest

A major sixth chord — a major triad with an added sixth. Gives a smooth, mellow, slightly jazzy colour without the more dissonant edge of a maj7. Common in jazz as a tonic substitute (often preferred over maj7 to avoid an awkward moving inner voice), and in soul, R&B, and vintage pop/doo-wop for a warm, resolved sound

A dominant ninth chord — a dominant seventh with an added ninth. Common in funk and soul for percussive, staccato chord stabs with a lush, extended colour beyond a plain dominant 7; also used in jazz as a richer substitute for a dominant 7 in ii-V-I progressions and applied dominants
